report.answer_text: French geographer Paul Vidal de la Blache laid the foundation of the school of possibilism in human geography. French historian Lucien Febvre later coined the term *possibilism*. (bsgi.it)

quotes.text: It is Febvre that will define it as Possibilistic Geography, a paradigm that will identify, up until the 1960s, the whole French geography.

context.before: highlighting Vidal’s epistemological foundations, substantially linked to spiritualism, contingentism, and neolamarckism, as well as how these foundations rest on five fundamental concepts: civilization and milieu are an inseparable pair whose combined action originates genres de vie, whereas landscape and region are the other inseparable pair originated by the action of a specific genre de vie.
context.after: This paradigm will be shaken by the emergence of theoretical-quantitative geography, which, owing to its nomothetic approach, will contrast its ideographic, purely descriptive approach, which is fundamentally pre-theoretic, and fixed on the description of landscape and region.

pages.quote_reason: The quote says Febvre defined possibilism as Possibilistic Geography, which backs his association with the concept, but it does not say he coined the term or that he was a historian.
